--- title: Identity and credential lifecycles — a password is not a session description: Build controlled accounts, Argon2id verification and opaque Bearer sessions in PostgreSQL; verify expiry, revocation, password changes, restarts and redaction. --- import { getIdentityExample } from '@/lib/js2py-examples' ## 1. A user_id in the database does not identify the caller The D labs accepted an owner_id to demonstrate relationships and transactions. That was an explicitly limited teaching input, not authentication. Any client can change JSON; TypeScript types, hidden buttons and CORS cannot prove identity. This chapter moves “who is calling?” out of the request body and into a credential verified by the service. The next chapter decides which objects that person may operate on. | Chapter contract | Scope | | --- | --- | | Prerequisites | D06: SQLAlchemy sessions, Alembic evolution and owned PostgreSQL tests; synchronous FastAPI, Pydantic, HTTP and fixtures | | New capabilities | Controlled provisioning, password hashing, login, server-side sessions, expiry, single/all-session revocation, password changes, disabling accounts and sensitive-error redaction | | Independent acceptance | Real PostgreSQL and HTTP reject incorrect, altered and expired credentials; changes and disabling invalidate old tokens; committed sessions survive restarts | | Not implemented | Public registration, email recovery, MFA, refresh tokens, object authorization or production TLS/rate/capacity guarantees | Download the [complete S01 lab](/learning-assets/js2py/s01-identity.zip). It includes three-language READMEs, sources, migrations, tests and an explicit packaging allowlist. It retains D's schema but **does not continue exposing D's self-reported-identity endpoints**. Each security lab is independent: no imports from another chapter and no connection to your existing database. The capstone mentions JWT as one possible design. Here we deliberately choose the user-approved alternative: an **opaque random session token**, not a partial JWT implementation. There are no client-readable identity claims; every request checks the database, making revocation easier to explain. The trade-off is dependence on session storage and its availability, with no offline verification. There is no refresh flow: log in again after expiry. ## 2. Separate four things before following a login ```text password -> Argon2id verify -> active user | random bearer returned once | DB: token digest + user_id + auth_version + expiry | next request: Bearer -> digest lookup -> user/version/expiry checks | authenticated actor ``` A **user record** represents an account, not a request. A **password** is a long-lived secret known to its user. A **password hash** lets the server verify a candidate without storing plaintext; it is not encrypted text that can be decrypted to recover the password. A **session token** is a temporary Bearer credential issued after login. Whoever possesses it may act through that session, so it is not an ordinary debugging string. A browser's loggedIn=true is only UI state. The service must independently verify each protected request. Hiding a logout button or forgetting to clear a client token must not change server-side revocation. A single login 200 does not establish permanent identity, much less permission to access someone else's project. ## 3. Start with a reviewable migration, not a default password Pinned baseline verified on **2026-09-28**: CPython 3.13.15, uv 0.12.13, FastAPI 0.135.1, Uvicorn 0.42.0, Pydantic 2.12.5, SQLAlchemy 2.0.54, Alembic 1.20.0, psycopg[binary] 3.3.6, PostgreSQL 18.6, argon2-cffi 25.1.0 and pytest 8.4.2. The real uv.lock resolves against public PyPI; these are tested pins, not a claim to use the latest releases. {getIdentityExample('pyproject.toml')} The complete migration chain retains 001_base, 002_expand and 003_contract, including the tasks.priority backfill and constraint, then adds 004_identity: {getIdentityExample('migrations/versions/004_identity.py')} Existing users have only id/login. A migration cannot magically make them legitimate login accounts. password_hash may be NULL, while existing users become is_active=false; a database check forbids an active account without a hash. auth_version starts at 1. For legacy records, created_at means migration time, not a fabricated historical signup date. password_changed_at is assigned only when a password is explicitly provisioned. auth_sessions stores only a token digest, the user foreign key, the authentication version at issuance, issued_at/expires_at and revoked_at. Indexes support user lookup and expiry maintenance; an index does not validate credentials. Time columns remain timestamptz, and existing RESTRICT foreign keys remain intact. Use upgrade head for a new database. An existing D database must first be checked against the exact matching 003_contract history; never blindly stamp an unversioned database. Security downgrades deliberately refuse to discard credential history automatically. Recovery needs a reviewed plan, not a version-number edit followed by running the old unauthenticated service. ## 4. Argon2id is not about turning passwords into strings quickly {getIdentityExample('security.py')} Read hasher, password_matches and login first; do not memorize the whole module at once. PasswordHasher comes from the established argon2-cffi library and explicitly selects Argon2id. Each hash call lets the library generate a random salt. The encoded string contains the salt, algorithm version, memory/iteration parameters and result. Give that encoded value and a candidate password to verify; do not split the format, compare a homemade password digest or design your own encryption. The fixed settings are m=65536 KiB, t=3 and p=4, matching the scale of the documented low-memory profile. Memory and computation raise the cost of offline guessing, but also consume server resources. Bigger parameters are not automatically better, and they are not a throughput promise. Measure on the deployment machine and pair the result with concurrency budgets and throttling. Two users choosing the same password should get different hashes; the lab actually tests this. After successful verification, check_needs_rehash determines whether to hash again with current parameters. Only then is the plaintext password available: the old hash cannot produce an “upgraded password.” Updating the hash encoding is not the same as a user password change; an actual password change increments auth_version. Unknown accounts also verify a startup-generated dummy hash, avoiding the obvious “no account, return immediately” branch. This **does not promise constant end-to-end timing**. A well-formed unknown-account login, wrong password and disabled account receive the same 401. Malformed input can still produce a sanitized 422; do not misclassify every failure as a database exception.
Explanation answer: why SHA-256 for token digests, but not passwords? Human-chosen passwords may be guessable. A fast hash makes offline guessing cheap; passwords need an established salted, adjustable-cost password hasher. A session token is generated by secrets.token_urlsafe(32), containing 32 random bytes, not a short password or user_id. SHA-256 supports lookup without storing that original token; it is not a homegrown password scheme. The stored digest itself is not accepted as a Bearer token, and the entry point validates the original token format. A database leak is nevertheless a security incident: digest-only storage does not remove access-control and backup-protection requirements.
## 5. Reestablish identity on every request Inside a transaction, login locks the user, verifies the password and active state, generates a random token, and stores its digest with the current auth_version. Only after commit does the endpoint return access_token. The default lifetime is 900 seconds, configurable within 60–3600. This example uses the application's UTC clock; production instances still need clock synchronization. UTC cannot repair an incorrect machine clock. authenticate parses Bearer syntax, hashes the original token, locates the session, locks the user, rereads the session, then checks active state, revoked_at, expiry and version equality. Every failure produces a generic 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer. Finding a digest is not the final check: an expired or revoked database row must still be rejected. Why document lock ordering in code? Ordinary requests take a shared user lock; password changes and all-session revocation take an exclusive lock. Further locks follow user, credential, project, task order. Revocation waits for already-started operations holding the relevant lock, and requests after its commit see the new version. It cannot pull an already-sent response back, and it is not a free concurrency optimization. The initial session lookup only locates the user; the session is reread after the user lock so stale discovery data is not the final decision. {getIdentityExample('db.py')} Each request owns its Session and transaction; never share one Session between threads. The engine is a connection-pool entry point, not a logged-in user session. auth_sessions is a business table. READ COMMITTED is explicit; echo is false and SQL parameters are hidden. These are three distinct meanings of “session.” ## 6. Inputs, responses and logs are separate leakage paths {getIdentityExample('schemas.py')} SecretStr masks common string representations, but login must still unwrap it with get_secret_value for verification. It does not encrypt HTTP, sanitize every exception automatically or manage shell history. New passwords must contain 15–128 characters, without trimming or implicit normalization. Length alone does not make a password safe; compromised-password screening and a complete account-recovery design remain release gates. {getIdentityExample('app.py')} Observe three output boundaries. UserPublic returns only id/login/is_active. TokenResponse returns the original Bearer only on successful login, with no-store/no-cache response headers. Validation errors retain only allowed loc components and type, never input, ctx, msg or the original body. Unknown field names are replaced too: a secret can appear as a JSON key, not just a value. Access logging is off; audit events contain fixed event names and server actor IDs, never submitted passwords, Bearers or Authorization. Integrity failures become generic 409 responses. Other SQLAlchemy failures become generic 503 responses without exception repr or traceback; hiding SQL parameters alone cannot make driver error text safe. Do not undo these boundaries with middleware that logs every request “for debugging.” Tests inspect both responses and real application/PostgreSQL logs. That is not automatic protection against future logging code or every unknown exception. ## 7. Start locally with a PostgreSQL cluster you own Work in the extracted s01-identity directory. The environment locations match the other labs in this round: ```bash export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH" export UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR=/tmp/langshift-js2py-python-20260928 export UV_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/langshift-js2py-uv-cache-20260928 unset VIRTUAL_ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT UV_ACTIVE UV_PYTHON UV_CONFIG_FILE export UV_NO_CONFIG=true uv sync --locked uv run --locked python labdb.py start ``` labdb.py creates a private mkdtemp directory and ownership marker, initializes PostgreSQL 18.6, and opens only a Unix socket inside that directory. It does not reuse PGDATA or connect to default localhost:5432. Before process/fixture connections are established, isolation.py clears every implicit PG* setting, including PGHOSTADDR and PGSERVICE. Database subprocesses also use a cleaned environment; overriding DATABASE_URL alone cannot establish isolation. Copy the printed DATABASE_URL export line into your terminal, then run: ```bash uv run --locked alembic upgrade head uv run --locked python admin.py create-user Alice uv run --locked python serve.py --port 8061 ``` The administrator command prompts twice through getpass. It accepts no password argument, repository default or default-password environment variable and prints no password. A legacy unprovisioned account can be explicitly activated; an already-provisioned account cannot be silently overwritten. There is no public registration endpoint. Real onboarding requires a trusted provisioning/first-change process, not temporary passwords in chat logs. {getIdentityExample('admin.py')} The API binds only to 127.0.0.1, uses one worker and has no reload. Missing configuration gives an error without printing the actual URL. /health/live proves only that the process responds; /health/ready additionally checks database availability and the migration revision, not overall security.
Answer: inspect the startup helper and safe cleanup {getIdentityExample('labdb.py')} This is readable isolation infrastructure, not an instruction to trust anything called a “test database.” Check the private directory, socket, version, ownership marker and actual postmaster data directory before permitting restart or stop. stop deletes the temporary data directory only after confirming this owned server has exited. restart preserves it. Never replace that logic with killing every postgres process, or experiment against the user's database.
## 8. Exercise the lifecycle with a client that does not print tokens Open another terminal in the same lab directory. The client sends only loopback requests, explicitly disables environment proxies with `ProxyHandler({})`, refuses redirects, prompts for passwords with getpass and stores tokens in a local mode-0600 session file without printing them. **Do not cat, commit or archive that file.** This is terminal-lab infrastructure, not advice to persist browser credentials in localStorage. A 127.0.0.1 URL alone is insufficient: urllib normally reads http_proxy, which could receive a local login password first. The regression sets proxy variables, removes no_proxy and uses owned loopback proxy/target listeners to prove the target receives requests while proxy and redirect-target counts remain zero. Do not assume OS defaults bypass the proxy. {getIdentityExample('client.py')} ```bash uv run --locked python client.py --port 8061 --session .session-alice.json login Alice uv run --locked python client.py --port 8061 --session .session-alice.json request GET /users/me cp -p .session-alice.json .session-before-change.json uv run --locked python client.py --port 8061 --session .session-alice.json change-password uv run --locked python client.py --port 8061 --session .session-before-change.json request GET /users/me ``` Expect login 200, public user retrieval 200, password change 204 with an empty body, and 401 when using the old copy. After a successful change the client deletes its current token file, but the server's auth_version increment is what invalidates all old tokens. Log in with the new password before testing revocation: ```bash uv run --locked python client.py --port 8061 --session .session-alice.json login Alice uv run --locked python client.py --port 8061 --session .session-alice.json request POST /auth/logout-all uv run --locked python client.py --port 8061 --session .session-alice.json request GET /users/me ``` The last request must be 401. /auth/logout revokes only the current session by setting revoked_at; another valid session remains usable. /auth/logout-all increments the account version and invalidates even the calling token. Passwords and tokens are not interchangeable; changing a password does not turn the old token into a new credential.
Lifecycle answer: does reenabling an account revive old tokens? No. The operator's disable sets is_active=false and increments auth_version; enable increments it again. An old session fails the version check even if it has not expired and revoked_at is still empty. A newly enabled user must log in to obtain a session at the current version. Deleting a browser token cannot replace server revocation, and changing only the password hash cannot invalidate previously issued sessions without a check such as this one.

The existing token must get 401 from /users/me, and login must also fail. After enable Alice, the old token must still fail; a fresh login succeeds. Tests actually perform both restarts. By contrast, labdb.py stop explicitly deletes the entire temporary data directory; intentional deletion is not a persistence failure. For final cleanup, stop your API first, then run uv run --locked python labdb.py stop. Delete only the session files you created; do not use broad cleanup globs in unfamiliar directories. Downloads use an explicit allowlist excluding sessions, environments, caches, logs and credentials. ## 10. Independent rebuild and active-session-count variation **Rebuild independently:** carry only the environment and migrations into a new directory. Implement the input/public models, hashing and session service, HTTP entry points and controlled provisioning command from this contract. Do not import the reference app. Acceptance includes wrong passwords, unknown accounts, altered and expired tokens, single/all-session revocation, password changes, disable/reenable, redaction and real restarts. Count only this user, this authentication version, unrevoked sessions and future expiry. Do not expose digests/tokens or count all historical rows. # Primary sources, version pins and local policy

核验 / Verified **2026-09-28**. This record applies to this independent lab.
Links below are primary project documentation, tagged project source or publisher
release metadata, retrieved over certificate-validated HTTPS. Live pages can
change. The shipped lock and executed PostgreSQL/HTTP cases define what was
actually verified; these pins are not advertised as the latest releases.

## Environment and resolution

- macOS arm64; CPython3.13.15; uv0.12.13; PostgreSQL18.6.
- Direct runtime pins: FastAPI0.135.1, Uvicorn0.42.0, Pydantic2.12.5,
  SQLAlchemy2.0.54, Alembic1.20.0, psycopg[binary]3.3.6, argon2-cffi25.1.0.
- Dev pin pytest8.4.2. `requires-python = ">=3.13,<3.14"`; `[tool.uv] package=false`.
- Real `uv lock --default-index https://pypi.org/simple` resolution and
  `uv sync --locked` installation. All registry entries are public PyPI,
  distribution URLs are files.pythonhosted.org and include real hashes.
- Locked runtime includes Starlette1.7.0, AnyIO4.15.1, pydantic-core2.41.5,
  argon2-cffi-bindings26.1.0 and h11 0.16.0. See uv.lock for the complete set.
- Release Python requirements are necessary compatibility checks, not proof of
  behavior. Real API/PG verification is recorded separately in VERIFICATION.md.

## Sources and precise claims

- [argon2-api](https://argon2-cffi.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api.html): Argon2id, per-hash random salt, verify exceptions and check_needs_rehash after successful verification.
- [argon2-parameters](https://argon2-cffi.readthedocs.io/en/stable/parameters.html): Explicit m=65536 KiB/t=3/p=4 profile; cost is not a capacity promise and must be measured on the target.
- [python-secrets](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/secrets.html): 32 explicit random bytes for token_urlsafe; random bearer, not user-selected password.
- [python-hashlib](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/hashlib.html): SHA-256 for high-entropy token lookup and validated-payload comparison, not password hashing.
- [python-datetime](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/datetime.html): Aware datetime and UTC normalization; timezone representation cannot repair clock skew.
- [python-decimal](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/decimal.html): String-to-Decimal construction and local precision context; no float-derived exact-money claim.
- [python-uuid](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/uuid.html): UUIDv4 operation identifiers; canonical syntax is a lab contract, not authorization.
- [owasp-passwords](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html): Use mature adaptive password hashing; production account-security gates remain separate.
- [owasp-sessions](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html): Session lifecycle, expiry, regeneration/revocation and protected transport.
- [owasp-authorization](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html): Deny by default, verify every request, and test object-level access with known IDs.
- [owasp-logging](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html): Exclude passwords, access tokens, session identifiers and sensitive connection details from logs.
- [postgres-isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html): READ COMMITTED statement snapshots, including a losing ON CONFLICT insertion whose winner requires a later SELECT.
- [postgres-locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/explicit-locking.html): Shared/exclusive row locks, ordering, blocking and deadlock boundaries.
- [postgres-insert](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-insert.html): ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING with an explicit unique target and RETURNING claim result.
- [postgres-constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html): Composite PK/FK/CHECK enforce data invariants, not caller authorization.
- [postgres-partial-indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-partial.html): A unique owner-only index proves at most one owner, not at least one.
- [sqlalchemy-transactions](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/session_transaction.html): The outer Session.begin owns commit/rollback; flush does not commit.
- [sqlalchemy-pg-insert](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/dialects/postgresql.html#insert-on-conflict-upsert): PostgreSQL dialect insert.on_conflict_do_nothing target and returning.
- [fastapi-errors](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/): Adapt request-validation and expected DB errors without echoing sensitive input.
- [pydantic-secrets](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/types/#pydantic.types.SecretStr): SecretStr masks common representations; get_secret_value unwraps intentionally, not transport encryption.
- [alembic-tutorial](https://alembic.sqlalchemy.org/en/latest/tutorial.html): Explicit revision history; no blind stamp or automatic destructive credential downgrade.
- [argon2-cffi](https://pypi.org/pypi/argon2-cffi/25.1.0/json): Publisher release 25.1.0; requires_python >=3.8.
- [SQLAlchemy](https://pypi.org/pypi/SQLAlchemy/2.0.54/json): Publisher release 2.0.54; requires_python >=3.7.
- [alembic](https://pypi.org/pypi/alembic/1.20.0/json): Publisher release 1.20.0; requires_python >=3.10.
- [psycopg](https://pypi.org/pypi/psycopg/3.3.6/json): Publisher release 3.3.6; requires_python >=3.10.
- [pytest](https://pypi.org/pypi/pytest/8.4.2/json): Publisher release 8.4.2; requires_python >=3.9.
- [fastapi-release](https://pypi.org/pypi/fastapi/0.135.1/json): Publisher release 0.135.1; requires_python >=3.10.
- [uvicorn-release](https://pypi.org/pypi/uvicorn/0.42.0/json): Publisher release 0.42.0; requires_python >=3.10.
- [pydantic-release](https://pypi.org/pypi/pydantic/2.12.5/json): Publisher release 2.12.5; requires_python >=3.9.
- [uv-release](https://pypi.org/pypi/uv/0.12.13/json): Publisher release 0.12.13; requires_python >=3.8.
- [python-release](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-31315/): Exact CPython 3.13.15 publisher release page; actual interpreter also checked locally.
- [postgres-release](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/release-18-6.html): Exact PostgreSQL18.6 release notes; actual SHOW server_version_num=180006 in every owned test cluster.
- [uv-package-tagged](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/uv/0.12.13/docs/concepts/projects/config.md): Tagged project configuration: package=false; environment used without packaging the lab.
- [uvicorn-settings-tagged](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Kludex/uvicorn/0.42.0/docs/settings.md): Tagged process/binding options; serve.py fixes loopback and disables access logs.

- [Python urllib.request](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/urllib.request.html): default environment proxy discovery, explicit `ProxyHandler({})` to disable it, and a no-redirect handler. A localhost URL alone does not protect credential routing.
- [PostgreSQL libpq environment](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/libpq-envars.html): implicit connection defaults including PGHOSTADDR/PGSERVICE; the lab clears PG* before opening connections and for owned database subprocesses.

## Retrieval failures and scope

The first Python Decimal and OWASP Authorization requests failed transient TLS
retrieval; retries succeeded with HTTP200. The uv settings endpoint returned403
and the legacy www.uvicorn.org settings endpoint failed TLS retrieval; official
tagged repository documentation was used instead. No certificate verification

UUIDv4 key, 86400-second receipt lifetime and retained-expired-key409 behavior
are **explicit course contracts**, not universal framework defaults. The capstone's
JWT suggestion is deliberately replaced by opaque DB-backed sessions in this
track. There is no refresh token, public registration or invented cryptography.
D migrations001–003 are preserved; no H done/note alias is smuggled into the D
project schema. No external side effects or production safety are inferred from
passing local tests. No API key or personal credential was accessed.

# Verification record — s01-identity

核验 / Executed **2026-09-28**, macOS arm64. This is local evidence, not a
production security audit or proof that untested integrations are safe.

## Executed source-tree acceptance

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH"
export UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR=/tmp/langshift-js2py-python-20260928
export UV_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/langshift-js2py-uv-cache-20260928
uv sync --locked
uv run --locked python -m pytest -q
```

Working directory: this lab root. The repository convenience runner is
`scripts/test-js2py-security-foundations.py`; shared test registration was not
edited. CPython3.13.15 / uv0.12.13 / PostgreSQL18.6; complete dependency pins are
in pyproject.toml and real public-PyPI uv.lock.

- **22 passed**, not merely compiled or imported.
- The fixture recorded **76 real loopback HTTP responses**. Status
  distribution: `{200: 43, 204: 5, 401: 20, 422: 6, 503: 2}`.
  This count excludes three additional real client.py subprocess requests
  (login, me, password change) whose outputs/private-file behavior were asserted.
- A fresh owned mkdtemp PostgreSQL cluster, private Unix socket, no TCP listening;
  server_version_num=180006 and READ COMMITTED were asserted.
- API process exited with 0; the owned cluster was stopped and its
  temporary root was confirmed absent after the run. No existing DB was selected.
- API and owned PostgreSQL restart tests verify committed state survives. Helper
  stop deliberately deletes the lab cluster and is not a persistence test.
- Application credential log scan: PASS. PostgreSQL credential log scan: PASS.
  No test credential values are published in this file or retained handoff evidence.

## Sensitive validation and error checks

Actual HTTP probes cover password too long, wrong JSON type, nested password value,
current/new password errors, short new password, malformed JSON and a secret marker
used as an unknown JSON field name. Returned errors retain only sanitized loc/type,
not input/ctx/msg/body or the unknown key. Tests check generic unknown-account,
wrong-password and disabled-account401, malformed/altered/expired Bearer401,
WWW-Authenticate, and token response no-store.

A real ALTER TABLE on the fixture-owned auth_sessions forces a database error:
GET /users/me returns generic503 without SQL/driver/credential details. The test
restores the table in finally and gets200 with the same still-valid token. A
wrong migration revision yields live200/ready503, then ready200 after restoration.
Private-client tests verify mode0600, refusal of a group/world-readable file,
getpass-based account creation and login/password-change output without secrets.

Application and PostgreSQL logs are scanned after process shutdown for generated
passwords, successful/altered Bearers and injected marker strings. Access logs are
disabled; audit records fixed events and server actor IDs only. SQL parameter
hiding is not treated as sufficient to sanitize driver messages; expected SQL
failures have explicit sanitized handlers. These probes are not a guarantee about
arbitrary new logging paths, every unknown exception, proxies or APM.

## Real revocation ordering

Two distinct PostgreSQL connections prove that disabling waits while an earlier
authenticated operation holds its shared user lock. pg_blocking_pids confirms an
actual wait, not a sleep-only guess. After the earlier transaction and disable
commit, the old credential gets401. Already-authorized work may finish; responses
already started cannot be retroactively canceled. Password changes/logout-all
increment auth_version; disable then enable does not revive old sessions.


## Final isolated-copy and actual CLI repetition

The final executable sources were copied from `s01-identity-files.json` into a fresh
allowlist-only directory (no .venv/session/cache/PGdata copied). The isolated
repository runner installed a new .venv and passed the same **22 cases**.
Across the three labs: **123 source-tree cases + 123 clean-copy cases**. A separate
`JS2PY_LAB_ROOT` single-extracted-root run passed **22 S01 cases**. These are
repeated executions, not 268 globally distinct test implementations.

```bash
python3 scripts/test-js2py-security-foundations.py --lab-root /path/to/extracted-parent --evidence-dir /path/to/redacted-evidence
JS2PY_LAB_ROOT=/path/to/extracted-single-lab python3 scripts/test-js2py-security-foundations.py --lab s01-identity
```

During the clean run, VIRTUAL_ENV/UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT pointed to an owned decoy,
UV_ACTIVE/UV_PYTHON/UV_CONFIG_FILE were deliberately invalid, UV_NO_CONFIG was
false, and PGHOSTADDR/PGSERVICE/PGDATABASE plus pytest argument/plugin overrides
were injected. The runner removed them, set no-config and explicit Python3.13.15,
retained only controlled Python/cache paths, and left the decoy sentinel directory
unchanged. It supports both `--lab-root` and `JS2PY_LAB_ROOT`, and refuses a .venv
symlink. It does not edit shared download/test registrations.

This lab also completed **14 actual client.py HTTP requests** from its clean copy,
using the default app entry (not just the solution entry used in pytest). Actual
labdb.py start/status-export/restart/stop were exercised with injected PG defaults.
API port conflict affected only the second owned process; the original remained
healthy. API and PG restarts retained committed state; final owned cleanup passed.
The three manual worksheets recorded **54 client requests** in total, separately
from pytest's recorded API requests and readiness polling.

## Independent-audit finding repaired and regressed

The read-only audit's P2 `SEC-S01-S03-001` correctly found that a loopback URL did
not prevent urllib's default environment proxy from receiving credentials. All
three clients now use `build_opener(ProxyHandler({}), NoRedirect())`. The fixture
HTTP client disables inherited proxies too. The new regression uses only owned
127.0.0.1 proxy, target and redirect listeners and synthetic credentials, with
proxy settings present and no_proxy absent: **target3 / proxy0 / redirect-target0**.
It asserts the target received the synthetic password/Bearer but writes no values
to evidence. No real proxy or personal credential is involved.

The separate libpq-isolation regression injects PGHOSTADDR/PGHOST/PGPORT/PGSERVICE/
PGSERVICEFILE/PGUSER/PGDATABASE/PGPASSWORD/PGOPTIONS, then successfully starts,
restarts and removes an owned PostgreSQL cluster. isolation.py clears PG* before
process/fixture connections; DB tools use a cleaned child environment. db.py and
migration env.py apply the same boundary for their independent CLI processes.

Final canonical files changed after the earlier read-only audit. The handoff
provides SHA-256 for every deliverable and a diff against the auditor's end
manifest. This is author regression evidence, **not a claim that an independent
review has already approved every final hash**. Core policy/transaction algorithms
were not rewritten by this fix. Shared-site build and TypeSafe remain owner work.

## Exclusions and integration boundary

Not verified: production TLS, login/body/rate limits, Argon2 load capacity,
compromised-password screening, public signup/recovery/MFA, cookie/CSRF design,
external logging/APM and every unknown exception, distributed clock skew,
production backup restore, RLS, ownership transfer, all deadlock/cleanup
interleavings, cross-service effects or exactly-once delivery. A readiness response
is not proof of these properties. Auth digests, password hashes and receipt data
still require controlled database/backup access.

The nine chapter locales are checked independently with installed MDX3/GFM and
React server rendering using in-memory loader substitution, plus exact ordered
code/source parity. That proves isolated document syntax/rendering, not shared
loader integration, Code Hike/site build, download ZIP generation or API correctness.
The owner integrates shared loaders/manifests/ZIPs/navigation/test registration.
No frontend dependency, API key, TypeSafe call, subagent or git commit was used.
